## Introduction

Welcome to Mini-Project #{{< meta mp_num >}}! In this mini-project, we will
explore patterns of *population density* within the United States, with an eye
towards identifying pockets of high density[^density] within the US and 
important ethnic enclaves. You are a freelance travel writer who has been 
hired to write an entry for a new travel publication, *Welcomed by the New
Colossus: An Atlas of American Communities*. Specifically, the editors have
asked you to write a two part story about a demographic group of interest to
you: they have given you full discretion to pick the topic, but they want you to
discuss both where that ethnic group lives in NYC and where they have 
concentrated in the broader USA. 

[^density]: Not surprisingly, NYC has many of the densest pockets of the US, but
the patterns outside of NYC may surprise you. For more, see {{< video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zFB5YooSo5M >}}

::: {.callout-note title="Choice of Demographic Group"}

Despite the title of this assignment, you **are not** required to focus on a 
demographic group with which you identify. Feel free to use any demographic 
group and to disclose as much or as little about yourself as you feel 
comfortable with while completing this assignment.

:::

Your analysis will principally rely on data from the 
[American Community Survey (ACS)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Community_Survey), 
the long-running premier national survey conducted by the US Census 
Bureau. Unlike the decadal census, which occurs once every ten years, the
ACS is constantly collecting new data, giving a up-to-date picture of the 
American public. ACS data is released across a range of granularities, from
national averages to small census-block level estimates. High-level estimates, 
*e.g.*, those for the country as a whole or individual states, are published on
a year-by-year basis, in a data product often called "ACS-1" since they are
derived from samples taken in a one-year window. In order to preserve respondent
privacy and ensure statistical reliability at finer scales, ACS estimates for 
smaller regions are published based on a rolling five-year window: these 
estimates are known as "ACS-5".[^lookback] Larger regions are also available 
from ACS-5 to avoid alignment issues, but these are a bit less useful to us. 

[^lookback]: Specifically ACS-5 estimates are computed over a retrospective 
(looking backwards) five year window: *e.g.*, the 2022 ACS-5 results are 
obtained by combining survey responses from 2018 to 2022. 

We will combine ACS estimates with data on NYC's built environment, available
to us via `PLUTO` (Primary Land Use Tax Output), NYC's primary database of 
buildings. By giving us additional information about the number of residential
units and the total residential square footage within each census block, this
will allow us to better understand how population density and demographic
concentration relate to residential density in NYC.

## Mini-Project #{{< meta mp_num >}}: {{< meta mp_title >}}

::: {.callout-caution title="Longest Mini-Project of the Semester"}

[Mini-Project #04](./mini04.qmd) will be shorter to give you sufficient

### Data Acquisition

When downloading data from a web-based resource, it is important to be a 
*polite* and *responsible* user of that resource. Specifically, we want to
avoid excessively and repeatedly re-downloading a file if it is not changing.
Running a public data source is costly and downloading a file 1,000 times when
you only need it once is simply abusing the good will of others. 

We can ensure responsible usage by adopting a practice of *file caching*:

- Create a "data directory" where data files relevant to the project can 
  be stored
- When attempting to load a data resource, first see if the relevant file is
  in the data directory:
  - If the file is in the data directory, simply read and return the contents of
    that file to the user
  - If the file is not in the data directory, download it into the data 
    directory and save a permanent copy for later use before reading and 
    returning the contents of the file to the user. 
    
This process of "saving" an intermediate result (data file) to avoid an expensive
step (downloading) is known as *caching*. Here, in addition to reducing load on
the data server, caching will also make your analysis faster (as you can avoid 
download times) and allow you to work even when you don't have reliable internet
access. 

Review the data download code I provided you in [MP#01](./mini01.qmd##data-acquisition) 
and [MP#02](./mini02.qmd##data-acquisition) to see how I implemented caching 
there. You should adopt similar patterns for this assignment. In particular,
you should consistently: 

1) Check if the results are available locally
2) If results are not available locally, download and save to a local file
3) Read results from the saved local file

Note that this pattern should be used *for all data access*, even if it's 
*via* a package like `tidycensus`. In addition to being polite, it will also
make your analysis run more quickly as you will not be constantly re-downloading
large data files. While it is possible to save your results in specialized
`R` data files, I recommend using open and transparent standards like `csv`
(`readr::read_csv()`) and `shp` (`sf::write_sf()`) as appropriate. 

#### Population Variables - Package Usage

Census data is very high-quality, but accessing it can be somewhat tricky The
census reports data in the form of "tables" which have systematic, but difficult
to interpret identifiers. We can access these using the `get_acs()` function 
from the `tidycensus` package, which works like this: 

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false
library(tidycensus)
library(gt)

ny_income <- get_acs(
    c(median_household_income="B19013_001"), 
    state="NY", 
    geography="county", 
    year=2018, 
    survey="acs1"
)
```

In this case, `B19013` is the table "Median Household Income in the Past 
12 Months (in YYYY Inflation-Adjusted Dollars)" and the suffix "001" indicates
that we want the first row of the table. Here, we asked for results from the
2018 ACS-1 county-level estimates for New York State. After
some basic formatting, we get the following results, which can be verified
against the [Census Data Explorer
website](https://data.census.gov/table?q=B19013&g=040XX00US36$0500000&y=2018):

```{r}
#| echo: false
ht <- function(x, n=3){
    rbind(head(x, n) |> mutate(.range="high"), 
          tail(x, n) |> mutate(.range="low"))
}
ny_income |> 
    select(-moe) |>
    pivot_wider(id_cols=c(GEOID, NAME), 
                names_from=variable, 
                values_from=estimate) |>
    arrange(desc(median_household_income)) |>
    ht(5) |>
    gt(id="tbl_income") |>
    cols_hide(".range") |> 
    tab_row_group(label="Lowest Median Household Income Counties", rows= .range == "low") |>
    tab_row_group(label="Highest Median Household Income Counties", rows= .range == "high") |>
    cols_label(median_household_income="Median Household Income") |>
    fmt_currency(median_household_income, 
                 currency="USD", 
                 decimals=0)
```

Here, the `GEOID`, also known as the FIPS code, is a unique identifier used for
different administrative units with the US (so states, counties, cities, *etc*
all have distinct `GEOID`s).  Note that I'm only showing the top and bottom 5 
counties here for brevity.

Unfortunately, relevant ancestry information is spread across several 
census tables that can be a bit difficult to use, including: 

- [`B04006`](https://data.census.gov/table?q=B04006) useful for European, 
  Carribean, and African ancestries
- [`B02018`](https://data.census.gov/table?q=B02018) useful for Asian ancestries
- [`B03001`](https://data.census.gov/table?q=B02018) useful for Latino ancestries

We can use these to compute the percent of residents of various NY counties
reporting certain ethnicities: 

```{r}
#| eval: false
get_acs(
    geography = "county",
    variables = c(
        korean = "B02018_005",
        irish="B04006_049",
        mexican="B03001_004",
        total = "B01003_001"
    ),
    state = "NY",
    year = 2024,
    survey = "acs5",
    output = "tidy"
) |>
    select(-moe) |> 
    pivot_wider(names_from=variable, values_from=estimate)
```

which gives the following: 

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
demo <- get_acs(
    geography = "county",
    variables = c(
        korean = "B02018_005",
        irish="B04006_049",
        mexican="B03001_004",
        total = "B01003_001"
    ),
    state = "NY",
    year = 2024,
    survey = "acs5",
    output = "tidy"
) |>
    select(-moe) |> 
    pivot_wider(names_from=variable, values_from=estimate) |> 
    mutate(pct_korean=korean/total, 
           pct_irish=irish/total,
           pct_mexican=mexican/total) |>
    slice_max(total, n=10)

demo |>
    gt() |>
    cols_hide(GEOID) |>
    cols_label(NAME="County",
               total="Total Population") |>
    fmt_number(c(total, korean, mexican, irish), 
               decimals=0) |>
    fmt_percent(starts_with("pct")) |>
    cols_merge(contains("korean"), pattern="{1} ({2})") |>
    cols_merge(contains("mexican"), pattern="{1} ({2})") |>
    cols_merge(contains("irish"), pattern="{1} ({2})") |>
    cols_label_with(c(korean, mexican, irish), 
                    \(x) paste0(str_to_title(x), "-American"))
```

If we want to extend to the ten most populous counties in the US as a whole,
we can pass `state.abb` (the 50 state codes) to the `state` argument of 
`get_acs()`:

```{r}
#| eval: false
get_acs(
    geography = "county",
    variables = c(
        korean = "B02018_005",
        irish="B04006_049",
        mexican="B03001_004",
        total = "B01003_001"
    ),
    state = state.abb,
    year = 2024,
    survey = "acs5") |>
    select(-moe) |> 
    pivot_wider(names_from=variable, values_from=estimate)
```

which gives the following: 

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
get_acs(
    geography = "county",
    variables = c(
        korean = "B02018_005",
        irish="B04006_049",
        mexican="B03001_004",
        total = "B01003_001"
    ),
    state = state.abb,
    year = 2024,
    survey = "acs5") |>
    select(-moe) |> 
    pivot_wider(names_from=variable, values_from=estimate) |> 
    mutate(pct_korean=korean/total, 
           pct_irish=irish/total,
           pct_mexican=mexican/total) |>
    slice_max(total, n=10) |>
    gt() |>
    cols_hide(GEOID) |>
    cols_label(NAME="County",
               total="Total Population") |>
    fmt_number(c(total, korean, mexican, irish), 
               decimals=0) |>
    fmt_percent(starts_with("pct")) |>
    cols_merge(contains("korean"), pattern="{1} ({2})") |>
    cols_merge(contains("mexican"), pattern="{1} ({2})") |>
    cols_merge(contains("irish"), pattern="{1} ({2})") |>
    cols_label_with(c(korean, mexican, irish), 
                    \(x) paste0(str_to_title(x), "-American"))
```

Note how we could use a _named vector_ as the first argument to `get_acs()` lets
us control the name the result is given in `R`. `get_acs()` has two additional
features that will be useful: 

- the ability to automatically download shapefile information associated with
  each result; 
- the ability to cache results automatically. 

You will want to use both of these in this assignment.

#### NYC Neighborhoods - File Download

For the second part of our analysis, where we look at patterns _within NYC_, we
will need to map census data to more interpretable neighborhoods. 
The NYC government recognizes approximately 250 neighborhoods as its official
_Neighborhood Tabulation Areas_. A shape file containing this information can
be found at 
<https://www.nyc.gov/content/planning/pages/resources/datasets/neighborhood-tabulation>.
Specifically, the first "Download Files" button just under `2020 Neighborhood
Tabulation Areas (NTAs)`. 

::: {.callout-tip title="Task 3: Data Acquisition - NYC NTAs"}

Write a function `load_nyc_nta()` which downloads the NTA shapefile, unzips
it, and reads it into `R` as an `sf` object. Your function should:

1) Create the directory `data/mp03` if it does not already exist. 
   (See previous MPs for examples of how this is done.)
   
2) Check if the NTA data is present in the `data/mp03` directory
   and, if it is not, download it using the `download.file()` function or
   the `httr2` package.
   
3) Unzip the downloaded `zip` file into a directory using the `unzip()` function.

4) Read the `shp` file in the unzipped directory into `R` using the `st()` 
   function from the `sf` package. 

5) Remove columns which you will not find helpful. 

6) Return the `sf` object to the caller.

:::

::: {.callout-caution title="Do Not Use `tidycensus` for NYC NTAs"}

It may be possible to get NTA level data and geometries using the `tidycensus` 
package: **Do not use `tidycensus` to access this data.** You must use generic
tools like the `download.file()` function or the `httr2` (not `httr`) package. 

The point of this portion is to practice getting data for which an easy wrapper
is not available. Use of `tidycensus` to access migration data will receive an
automatic 0 for the "Data Preparation" portion of this mini-project and 
significant penalization on the "Project Skeleton" portion. 

:::

#### Aggregating Tract Data to NTAs

Now that you have NYC's NTA map, we can _aggregate_ our population counts from
tract level to neighborhood level. To do this, we need to _join_ these two data
sets together, but this is not a typical join. Because our join is based on
'is this tract in this NTA?' rather than (scalar) equality, we need to use
a _spatial_ join, which we implement via the `sf::st_join` function. 
This join requires a slightly different syntax, including 
specification of the 'check' used to align rows: 

- `st_contains`: Does the spatial region in the first table contain the points
  in the second table? (Regions first argument, points second argument)
- `st_intersects`: Does a point from the first table fall in a region from the
  second table? (Points first argument, regions second argument)
  
These functions are passed (without parentheses or any arguments) as the 
`join` argument of `st_join`. Either of these can work for this step; you simply
need to make sure you're passing the `join` that corresponds to the order of the
tables. A naive join, however, can result in _too many_ rows if a tract crosses
multiple NTAs. (This is likely as the Census and the City do not coordinate 
these boundaries.) We will instead just assign each tract to the NTA with which
it has the _largest_ intersection, using the `largest=TRUE` argument to 
`st_join`. 

After joining these data sets, we can use `st_drop_geometry()` to temporarily
drop the geometry and summarize our data as usual.[^drop] Finally, we can join 
our summarized census data with our original NTA data to connect it back to the
shape information. 


[^drop]: If you don't drop the geometry column first, you have to combine
`geometry` elements during your `summarize` step. This is slow and unwieldy, so
it's far easier to drop, summarize, and then join back to the original data.


::: {.callout-tip title="Task 4: Aggregate Tract Data to the NTA Level"}

Following the strategy above, aggregate your census tract population variables
to the NTA level. Make sure that you 'reconnect' these aggregate values to 
the NTA geometry for later use.

:::

#### NYC PLUTO - API Usage

Finally, we need to download the [PLUTO data from NYC OpenData](https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/Primary-Land-Use-Tax-Lot-Output-PLUTO-/64uk-42ks/about_data) using the provided API. To access this API, 
click "Export" near the top right corner of the page, then select "API endpoint",
"Data Format: CSV", and "Version: SODA2" to get the _base URL_ for this API. 

By default, if you simply download directly from that URL you will only get
the first 1000 rows in the data set. To download the full data set, you will
need to adjust the `$limit` and `$offset` parameters in your API call. The

- `$limit` controls the number of results returned per query. It defaults 
   to 1000, but can be set much larger than this. Note that you do not 
   necessarily want to set `$limit` *too large* as this decreases download times
   and increases the chance of corruption or time-outs during download. 
- `$offset` adjusts the results returned from a query. It defaults to 0, 
   returning items 1 to 1000 (at the default `$limit` of 1000). If you set
   `$offset` to 1000, you will instead retrieve rows 1001 to 2000 (at the
   default `$limit` of 1000). By iteratively adjusting `$offset`, you can 
   "page through" the entire data set. 
   
   If there are not `$limit` results remaining, you will get only as many 
   results as can be returned after the offset. So, in a data set of 1500 
   observations, a query with `$limit=1000` and `$offset=1000` will return
   rows 1001 to 1500. The fact that this is less than `$limit` can be used
   to identify the end of the data set. 
   
Using these two query parameters you will be able to download the NYC PLUTO
data _responsibly_. 

::: {.callout-tip title="Task 5: Download PLUTO"}

Write a function to download the NYC PLUTO data _correctly_, _completely_ and 
_responsibly_. When this function is called, it should 

i)   Check if the data is already available locally and use the cached copy
     if available. 
ii)  Download the PLUTO data in a _paginated_ fashion using the two API 
     parameters listed above. 
iii) Combine all API responses using the `bind_rows()` function from the `dplyr` 
     package. 
iv)  Save the combined data set as a `csv` for later use that can be read with
     `readr::read_csv()`

Feel free to save only those columns of the PLUTO data that you will need for
later analyses. Alternatively, keep them all in your cached `csv`, but only read
in necessary columns using the `col_select` argument to `readr::read_csv()`.

*Hint*: [This old Mini-Project](https://michael-weylandt.com/STA9750/archive/AY-2024-SPRING/miniprojects/mini01.html#acquiring-payroll-data) may be helpful.
     
:::

### Data Cleaning and Preparation 

You should have completed your data cleaning as part of the 
import steps above. While it is generally good to "spot check" data for accuracy,
in this case we can trust the Census Bureau and NYC and move immediately to EDA,

### Data Integration and Initial Exploration {#eda}

::: {.callout-tip title="Task 6: Exploratory Data Analysis"}

Answer the following questions to perform your Exploratory Data Analysis of the
various data sets used in this project. For each question, answer using inline
values, a table, or a graphic as you feel is most effective, though you
should plan to have _at least_: 2 tables, 2 inline values, 1 non-spatial plot, 
1 spatial plot among your several answers. 

Note that you will need to determine which data sets are best suited to answer 
each question and may need to return to earlier steps and acquire more
data:[^invalidation] some questions might require joining multiple data sets to
answer fully. 

01. Which NYC census tract has the most office floor area in NYC? 

    *Hint*: Use the `bct2020` column of the PLUTO data to get census tract ID
    and the `officearea` column to get office area. I think you can safely treat
    `NA` values in office area as 0s. 
    
02. Which NYC NTA has the most residential units (`unitsses` in PLUTO)? 
03. Which NYC census tract has the highest population density, measured as 
    population per square foot of residential space? Do your answers change if
    you measure by population per residential unit?
04. What 5 metro areas, other than NYC, have the largest share of population that 
    identify with your ancestry of interest? 
   
05. At a not-too-granular level, describe the distribution of ancestries in a 
    large non-NYC city of your choosing from the previous question.
06. As a percentage of all US residents who identify with your ancestry of 
    interest, how many live in NY and how many live in other major metro areas?
    
    *Hint*: `get_acs(geography="us")` will be helpful to get the 
    denominator here.
07. Do we observe a roughly linear relationship between population and
    housing (units or area) across NYC tracts or is the relationship 
    more complex?
08. What are the NTAs with highest buildings? (You can use PLUTO's `numfloors`
    variable as a measure of height. You don't need to get actual physical 
    measurements.) 
09. Visualize how population density varies across NYC?
10. How many New Yorkers live in areas that could be described as 'primarily
    commercial'? (This one is particularly open-ended.)

:::

[^invalidation]: Depending on what additional data you need and how exactly you
structure your code, you might need to _delete_ your cached data file to force
a re-download with the additional variables. The question of knowing when to
delete the cache is known as _cache invalidation_ and it is a hard problem in
computer science and system design.

### Final Deliverable: Atlas of Communities Entry

Now that your data is fully prepared, it's time to write your entry for
*Welcomed by the New Colossus*. Write an overview and brief story about
"X"-Americans, discussing where they live in NYC and where they can be found
throughout the US. Your write up should include at least 4 numerical facts and
two maps of your choosing. (These can be, but are not required to be, related
to the EDA performed above.) Make sure to include relevant historical context
as well. This should be _at least_ 300 words, but you can use more if you have
more information to add. 


::: {.callout-tip title="Task 7: Atlas of American Communities Entry"}

Write up your entry for the Atlas of American Communities. It should contain
(at least) the items noted above, but you can have as much fun with this and 
go as deep into the subject as you want. 

:::

### Extra Credit Opportunity #01: Interactive Graphics {#ec01}

**Possible Extra Credit: Up to 3 Points**

One point of extra credit will be awarded to submissions that make effective 
use of the "interactive" functionality afforded by the `ggiraph` package in a 
standard (non-map) graph; an additional point of extra credit will be awarded
for use of interactive functionality on a map. 
(See [Lab #07](../labs/lab07.qmd#interactive) for examples.) 
A final (third) point of extra credit will be awarded for effective 
visualizations that use the `data_id` functionality in conjunction with 
the `patchwork` package to link _across_ different panels in a visualization.

### Extra Credit Opportunity #02: Additional Census Tables {#ec02}

**Possible Extra Credit: Up to 3 Points**

Up to three points of extra credit will be awarded for analyses that use 
additional (non-ancestry) census data tables in a manner that enriches your 
final write up. 

The [Census Data Explorer](https://data.census.gov/) can help you find relevant
tables, but your favorite LLM will likely be more effective than trying to 
navigate through the census tables directly. I would however, **strongly** advise
you to cross-check things. The specific census table codes are not the kind of 
data that is well-represented in LLM training data and I have found them to be
wrong with surprising regularity.
